Aadan.desc: Possibly a Somali form of Adam.

Aafje.desc: Short form of names beginning with the Old German element alb "elf".

Aage.desc: Danish and Norwegian form of Áki.

Aaliyah.desc: Feminine form of Aali. It was popularized in the English-speaking world by the singer Aaliyah Haughton (1979-2001), who was known simply as Aaliyah. This name received a boost in popularity after she released her debut album in 1994, and also in 2001 after her untimely death in an airplane crash.

Aamina.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic آمنة (see Aminah 1), as well as the Somali form.

Aaminah.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic آمنة (see Aminah 1).

Aamir 1.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عامر (see 'Aamir), as well as the usual Urdu transcription.

Aang.desc: The hero of the American animated television series Avatar: The Last Airbender (2005-2008). When his name is shown in written form, it is composed of the Chinese characters 安 (ān) meaning "peace, quiet" and 昂 (áng) meaning "raise, lift".

Aaralyn.desc: Feminine elaboration of Aaron using the popular name suffix lyn.

Aaren.desc: Variant or feminine form of Aaron.

Aarne.desc: Finnish and Estonian form of Arne 1.

Aarni.desc: Finnish form of Arne 1, also associated with the archaic word aarni meaning "treasure".

Aaro.desc: Finnish and Estonian form of Aaron.

Aaron.desc: From the Hebrew name אַהֲרֹן ('Aharon), which is most likely of unknown Egyptian origin. Other theories claim a Hebrew derivation, and suggest meanings such as "high mountain" or "exalted". In the Old Testament this name is borne by the older brother of Moses. He acted as a spokesman for his brother when they appealed to the pharaoh to release the Israelites from slavery. Aaron's rod produced miracles and plagues to intimidate the pharaoh. After the departure from Egypt and arrival at Mount Sinai, God installed Aaron as the first high priest of the Israelites and promised that his descendants would form the priesthood.... [more]

Aarre.desc: Means "treasure" in Finnish. It may also be used as a variant of the uncommon older name Aaretti, itself from a Low German form of Arnold.

Aarti.desc: From the name of a Hindu ritual in which offerings of lamps or candles are made to various gods, derived from Sanskrit आरात्रिक (aratrika).

Aatto.desc: Finnish form of Adolf. It also means "eve, evening before" in Finnish, as the day before an important holiday.

Abaddon.desc: Means "ruin, destruction" in Hebrew. In Revelation in the New Testament this is another name of the angel of the abyss.

Abbán.desc: Means "little abbot", derived from Irish abb "abbot" combined with a diminutive suffix. This was the name of a 6th-century Irish saint, the son of King Cormac of Leinster.

'Abbas.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic/Persian عبّاس (see Abbas).

Abbas.desc: Means "austere" in Arabic. This was the name of the Prophet Muhammad's uncle. It was also borne by a son of Ali, the fourth caliph.

Abd al-Aziz.desc: Means "servant of the powerful" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with عزيز ('aziz) meaning "powerful". This was the name of the first king of modern Saudi Arabia.

Abd al-Hamid.desc: Means "servant of the praiseworthy" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with حَمِيد (hamid) meaning "praiseworthy". This was the name of two sultans of the Ottoman Empire.

Abd al-Haqq.desc: Means "servant of the truth" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with حقّ (haqq) meaning "truth".

Abd al-Kader.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد القادر (see Abd al-Qadir).

Abd al-Karim.desc: Means "servant of the generous" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with كَرِيم (karim) meaning "generous".

Abd Allah.desc: Means "servant of Allah" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with الله (Allah). This was the name of the Prophet Muhammad's father. He died before his son's birth.

Abd al-Latif.desc: Means "servant of the gentle" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with لطيف (latif) meaning "gentle".

Abd al-Majid.desc: Means "servant of the glorious" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with مجيد (majid) meaning "glorious".

Abd al-Malik.desc: Means "servant of the king" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with ملك (malik) meaning "king". This was the name of the fifth Umayyad caliph, who made Arabic the official language of the empire.

Abd al-Qadir.desc: Means "servant of the capable, servant of the powerful" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with قادر (qadir) meaning "capable, powerful". This was the name of a 19th-century Algerian resistance leader.

Abd al-Rahim.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرحيم (see Abd ar-Rahim).

Abd al-Rahman.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرحمٰن (see Abd ar-Rahman).

Abd al-Rashid.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرشيد (see Abd ar-Rashid).

Abd al-Salam.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد السلام (see Abd as-Salam).

Abd al-Wali.desc: Means "servant of the guardian" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with ولِي (wali) meaning "guardian, friend".

Abd ar-Rahim.desc: Means "servant of the merciful" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with رحيم (rahim) meaning "merciful".

Abd ar-Rahman.desc: Means "servant of the merciful" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with رحمن (rahman) meaning "merciful". This was the name of two early caliphs of the Umayyad dynasty in Spain.

Abd ar-Rashid.desc: Means "servant of the rightly guided" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with رَشِيد (rashid) meaning "rightly guided".

Abd as-Salam.desc: Means "servant of the peaceful" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with سلام (salam) meaning "peace".

Abdastartus.desc: From the Greek form Ἀβδάσταρτος (Abdastartos) of the Phoenician name 𐤏𐤁𐤃𐤏𐤔𐤕𐤓𐤕 (ʿAbdʿashtart) meaning "servant of Ashtoreth", derived from 𐤏𐤁𐤃 (ʿabd) meaning "servant, slave" combined with the name of the goddess Ashtoreth. This was the name of a 10th-century BC king of Tyre, as recorded by the historian Josephus.

Abdelaziz.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد العزيز (see Abd al-Aziz) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abdelhak.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الحقّ (see Abd al-Haqq) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abdelhamid.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الحميد (see Abd al-Hamid) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abdelkader.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد القادر (see Abd al-Qadir) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abdellatif.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد اللطيف (see Abd al-Latif) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abdelmajid.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد المجيد (see Abd al-Majid) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abderrahim.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرحيم (see Abd ar-Rahim) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abderrahmane.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرحمٰن (see Abd ar-Rahman) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abdeslam.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد السلام (see Abd as-Salam) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abdessalam.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد السلام (see Abd as-Salam) chiefly used in Northern Africa.

Abdias.desc: Form of Obadiah used in the Greek and Latin Old Testament, as well as the Portuguese form (used chiefly in Brazil).

Abdiel.desc: Means "servant of God" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament, this is the name of a member of the tribe of Gad. In John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667), this is the name of a seraph who withstands Satan when he urges the angels to revolt.

Abdiou.desc: Form of Obadiah used in the Greek Old Testament, also spelled Ἀβδίας (Abdias).

Abdolhossein.desc: Means "servant of al-Husayn" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with حسّین (Hosseyn), the Persian form of Arabic Husayn. This name refers to Husayn ibn Ali, the son of Ali.

Abdolreza.desc: Means "servant of al-Ridha" from Arabic عبد ('abd) meaning "servant" combined with رضا (Reza), the Persian form of Arabic Ridha. This name refers to the 9th-century Shia imam Ali al-Ridha.

Abdou.desc: Form of Abduh common in western and northern Africa.

Abdoul.desc: Form of Abdul used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.

Abdoulaye.desc: Form of Abd Allah used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.

Abdul.desc: First part of compound Arabic names beginning with عبد ال ('Abd al) meaning "servant of the" (such as عبد العزيز ('Abd al-'Aziz) meaning "servant of the powerful").

Abdul Aziz.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد العزيز (see Abd al-Aziz).

Abdulaziz.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد العزيز (see Abd al-Aziz).

Abdul Hamid.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الحميد (see Abd al-Hamid).

Abdul Haq.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الحقّ (see Abd al-Haqq), as well as the usual Urdu transcription.

Abdulla.desc: Form of Abd Allah in several languages, as well as an alternate transcription of the Arabic name.

Abdullah.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الله (see Abd Allah), as well as the regular form in several other languages.

Abdullo.desc: Tajik and Uzbek form of Abd Allah.

Abdullohi.desc: Tajik variant form of Abd Allah.

Abdul Rahman.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرحمٰن (see Abd ar-Rahman), as well as the regular Malay form.

Abdur Rahim.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرحيم (see Abd ar-Rahim).

Abdur Rahman.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرحمٰن (see Abd ar-Rahman), as well as the usual Bengali transcription.

Abdur Rashid.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الرشيد (see Abd ar-Rashid), as well as the usual Bengali transcription.

Abdus Salam.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد السلام (see Abd as-Salam), as well as the usual Bengali transcription.

Abe 2.desc: Originally a Frisian short form of Adalbert (and other names starting with the Old German element adal "noble" and a second element beginning with b).

Abednego.desc: Means "servant of Nebo" in Akkadian, Nebo being the Babylonian god of wisdom. In the Old Testament Abednego is the Babylonian name given to Azariah, one of the three men cast into a blazing furnace but saved from harm by God, as told in the Book of Daniel.

Abel.desc: From the Hebrew name הֶבֶל (Hevel) meaning "breath". In the Old Testament he is the second son of Adam and Eve, murdered out of envy by his brother Cain. In England, this name came into use during the Middle Ages, and it was common during the Puritan era.

Abene.desc: Derived from Basque abe meaning "pillar". It is a Basque equivalent of Pilar.

Abeni.desc: Means "we prayed and we received" in Yoruba.

Aberash.desc: Means "giving off light, shining" in Amharic.

Abhijeet.desc: Alternate transcription of Hindi/Marathi अभिजीत or अभिजित or Bengali অভিজিৎ (see Abhijit).

Abhijit.desc: From Sanskrit अभिजित (abhijita) meaning "victorious". This is the Sanskrit name for the star Vega.

Abia.desc: Biblical Greek and Latin form of Abijah.

Abiah.desc: Variant of Abijah, which also appears in the English Bible.

Abiathar.desc: From Hebrew אֶבְיָתָר ('Evyatar) meaning "my father abounds" or "my father excels". In the Old Testament Abiathar was a high priest during the reign of King David.

Abidan.desc: Means "my father is judge" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament he is a Benjamite prince.

Abidemi.desc: Means "born in my absence" in Yoruba. It is typically given to children born when the father is away.

Abiel.desc: Means "God is my father" in Hebrew. This was the name of the grandfather of Saul in the Old Testament.

Abigail.desc: From the Hebrew name אֲבִיגָיִל ('Avigayil) meaning "my father is joy", derived from the roots אָב ('av) meaning "father" and גִּיל (gil) meaning "joy". In the Old Testament this is the name of Nabal's wife. After Nabal's death she became the third wife of King David.... [more]

Abihu.desc: Means "he is my father" in Hebrew. This is the name of a son of Aaron in the Old Testament. He and his brother Nadab were killed by God because they presented him with unauthorized fire.

Abijah.desc: Means "my father is Yahweh" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament this is the name of several characters, both male and female, including the second king of Judah (also known as Abijam).

Abilene.desc: From a place name mentioned briefly in the New Testament. It is probably from Hebrew אָבֵל ('avel) meaning "meadow, grassy area". It has occasionally been used as a given name in modern times.

Abimael.desc: Meaning uncertain, though the first element is likely Hebrew אָב ('av) meaning "father". In the Old Testament he is listed as a descendant of Shem.

Abimbola.desc: Means "born to me with wealth" in Yoruba.

Abimelech.desc: Means "my father is king" in Hebrew, derived from the roots אָב ('av) meaning "father" and מֶלֶכְ (melekh) meaning "king". This is the name of several characters in the Old Testament including a king of Gerar who takes Abraham's wife Sarah, but is forced by God to give her back.

Abiodun.desc: Means "born on a festival" in Yoruba.

Abiram.desc: Means "my father is exalted" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament, Abiram is swallowed by an earthquake after rebelling against the leadership of Moses.

Abishag.desc: Means "my father strays" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament Abishag is a young woman who tends King David in his old age.

Abishai.desc: Means "my father is a gift" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament he is one of King David's heroes.

Abital.desc: Means "my father is dew" in Hebrew. She is the fifth wife of David in the Old Testament.

'Abla.desc: Means "full-figured" in Arabic. The 7th-century Arabic poet Antara dedicated much of his poetry to a woman named Abla.

Abner.desc: Means "my father is a light" in Hebrew, from אָב ('av) meaning "father" and נֵר (ner) meaning "lamp, light". In the Old Testament, Abner was a cousin of Saul and the commander of his army. After he killed Asahel he was himself slain by Asahel's brother Joab.... [more]

Abosede.desc: Means "comes with the start of the week" in Yoruba, given when the child is born on Sunday.

Aboubacar.desc: Form of Abu Bakr used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.

Abraam.desc: Biblical Greek form of Abraham, as well as a Georgian form.

Abraham.desc: This name may be viewed either as meaning "father of many" in Hebrew or else as a contraction of Abram 1 and הָמוֹן (hamon) meaning "many, multitude". The biblical patriarch Abraham was originally named Abram but God changed his name (see Genesis 17:5). With his father Terah, he led his wife Sarah, his nephew Lot and their other followers from Ur into Canaan. He is regarded by Jews as being the founder of the Hebrews through his son Isaac and by Muslims as being the founder of the Arabs through his son Ishmael.... [more]

Abram 1.desc: Means "high father" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament God changed Abram's name to Abraham (see Genesis 17:5).

Abram 2.desc: Russian and Georgian form of Abraham.

Abrar.desc: Means "virtuous" in Arabic. It is typically feminine in the Arab world, and typically masculine in Pakistan, India and Bangladesh.

Abril.desc: Spanish and Catalan form of April.

Absalom.desc: From the Hebrew name אַבְשָׁלוֹם ('Avshalom) meaning "my father is peace", derived from אָב ('av) meaning "father" and שָׁלוֹם (shalom) meaning "peace". In the Old Testament he is a son of King David. He avenged his sister Tamar by arranging the murder of her rapist, their half-brother Amnon. He later led a revolt against his father. While fleeing on the back of a mule he got his head caught in a tree and was killed by Joab.

Abu.desc: Means "father of" in Arabic. This is commonly used as an element in a kunya, which is a type of Arabic nickname. The element is combined with the name of one of the bearer's children (usually the eldest son). In some cases the kunya is figurative, not referring to an actual child, as in the case of the Muslim caliph Abu Bakr.

Abu al-Fadl.desc: Combination of Abu and Fadl. This was another name for Abbas, the son of the fourth caliph Ali.

Abubakar.desc: Form of Abu Bakr used in Nigeria.

Abu Bakr.desc: Combination of Abu and Bakr. Abu Bakr was a companion and father-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad and the first caliph of the Muslim world. His name was in fact a kunya (a nickname) formed using Abu; his real name was Abd Allah. Shia Muslims hold a more negative view of Abu Bakr, hence this name is more widely used among Sunnis.

Abul-Fazl.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic أبو الفضل (see Abu al-Fadl).

Abundius.desc: From Latin abundus meaning "abundant, plentiful". This was the name of several early saints, including a 5th-century bishop of Como.

Aca.desc: Serbian and Macedonian diminutive of Aleksandar.

Acacia.desc: From the name of a type of tree, ultimately derived from Greek ἀκή (ake) meaning "thorn, point".

Acantha.desc: Latinized form of Greek Ἄκανθα (Akantha), which meant "thorn, prickle". In Greek legend she was a nymph loved by Apollo.

Ace 1.desc: From the English word meaning "highest rank". More commonly a nickname, it is occasionally used as a given name.

Achab.desc: Latin form of Ahab used in some versions of the Vulgate.

Achaemenes.desc: Latin form of Ἀχαιμένης (Achaimenes), the Greek form of the Old Persian name 𐏃𐎧𐎠𐎶𐎴𐎡𐏁 (Haxamaniš), derived from Old Iranian *haxa "friend, companion, ally" and *manah "mind, intellect, thought". This was the name of the founder of the Achaemenid dynasty (7th century BC).

Achaicus.desc: Latinized form of the Greek name Ἀχαϊκός (Achaikos), which referred to the region in Greece called Ἀχαΐα (Achaia), situated on the northern coast of the Peloponnese. In the New Testament this is the name of a Corinthian Christian who aids Saint Paul.

Achan.desc: Possibly a variation of the Hebrew word עֲכָר ('akhar) meaning "trouble". In the Old Testament, Achan is stoned to death because he steals forbidden items during the assault on Jericho.

Achelous.desc: From Greek Ἀχελώιος (Acheloios), which is of unknown meaning, possibly of Semitic origin. This was the name of a Greek god of water and rivers, in particular the Achelous River in western Greece. He fought with (and was defeated by) Herakles for the hand of Deianeira.

Achille.desc: French and Italian form of Achilles.

Achilles.desc: From the Greek Ἀχιλλεύς (Achilleus), which is of unknown meaning, perhaps derived from Greek ἄχος (achos) meaning "pain" or else from the name of the Achelous River. This was the name of a warrior in Greek legend, one of the central characters in Homer's Iliad. The bravest of the Greek heroes in the war against the Trojans, he was eventually killed by an arrow to his heel, the only vulnerable part of his body.... [more]

Achim 2.desc: Possibly means "he will establish" in Hebrew. In the New Testament this name is listed as an ancestor of Jesus.

Achsah.desc: Means "anklet, bangle" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament this is the name of the daughter of Caleb.

Aco.desc: Macedonian and Serbian diminutive of Aleksandar.

Ada 1.desc: Originally a short form of Germanic names such as Adelaide or Adelina that begin with the element adal meaning "noble". Saint Ada was a 7th-century Frankish abbess at Le Mans. This name was also borne by Augusta Ada King (1815-1852), the Countess of Lovelace (known as Ada Lovelace), a daughter of Lord Byron. She was an assistant to Charles Babbage, the inventor of an early mechanical computer.

Adad-Nirari.desc: Means "Adad is my helper", from the god's name Adad combined with Akkadian nērāru meaning "helper". This name was borne by three kings of the Assyrian Empire.

Adaeze.desc: Means "eldest daughter of the king" in Igbo.

Adah.desc: Means "adornment, ornament" in Hebrew. This was the name of the wives of both Lamech and Esau in the Old Testament.

Adaiah.desc: From the Hebrew name עֲדָיָה ('Adayah) meaning "Yahweh has adorned". This is the name of numerous Old Testament characters, including the father of Jedidah.

Adair.desc: From an English surname that was derived from the given name Edgar.

Adalbern.desc: Derived from the Old German elements adal "noble" and bern "bear".

Adalbert.desc: Old German form of Albert. This is the name of a patron saint of Bohemia, Poland and Prussia. He is known by his birth name Vojtěch in Czech and Wojciech in Polish.

Adalet.desc: Means "justice" in Turkish, ultimately from Arabic عَدَلَ ('adala) meaning "to act justly".

Adalfarus.desc: Derived from the Old German elements adal "noble" and fara "journey".

Adalgund.desc: Derived from the Old German elements adal "noble" and gunda "battle". See also Aldegund.

Adalhard.desc: Derived from the Old German elements adal "noble" and hart "hard, firm, brave, hardy". Saint Adalhard or Adalard was a cousin of Charlemagne who became an abbot of Corbie.

Adalia.desc: Meaning unknown, possibly of Persian origin. In Book of Esther in the Old Testament this is the name of a son of Haman the Agagite.

Adallinda.desc: Derived from the Old German elements adal "noble" and lind "soft, flexible, tender". Adallinda (or Adalindis or Ethelind) was the name of one of the concubines of Charlemagne, with whom she had at least two children.

Adalwin.desc: From the Old German elements adal "noble" and wini "friend" (a cognate of Æðelwine).

Adalyn.desc: Variant of Adeline using the popular name suffix lyn.

Adalynn.desc: Variant of Adeline using the popular name suffix lynn.

Adam.desc: This is the Hebrew word for "man". It could be ultimately derived from Hebrew אדם ('adam) meaning "to be red", referring to the ruddy colour of human skin, or from Akkadian adamu meaning "to make".... [more]

Adamantios.desc: Derived from Greek ἀδάμας (adamas) meaning "unconquerable, unbreakable, adamant" (genitive ἀδάμαντος).

Adamou.desc: Form of Adam used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.

Adamu.desc: Old Church Slavic form of Adam.

Adanna.desc: Means "eldest daughter of the father" in Igbo.

Adannaya.desc: Means "eldest daughter of her father" in Igbo.

Adas.desc: Short form of names beginning with Ad, such as Adomas or Adolfas.

Adawosgi.desc: Means "he is swimming" in Cherokee, from ᎠᏓᏬᏍᎬ (adawosgun) meaning "swimming".

Addie.desc: Diminutive of Adelaide, Adeline, Addison and other names containing the same sound.

Addilyn.desc: Variant of Adeline using the popular name suffix lyn.

Addison.desc: From an English surname meaning "son of Adam". Its recent popularity as a feminine name stems from its similarity in sound to Madison.

Addolorata.desc: Means "grieving" in Italian, from the title of the Virgin Mary, Maria Addolorata. It is most common in southern Italy. It is the equivalent of Spanish Dolores.

Addy 1.desc: Diminutive of Adelaide, Adeline, Addison and other names containing the same sound.

Ade 1.desc: From Yoruba adé meaning "crown", also a short form of other names beginning with this element.

Ade 2.desc: Originally a short form of Germanic names beginning with the element adal meaning "noble".

Adebayo.desc: Means "the crown meets joy" in Yoruba.

Adebola.desc: Means "the crown meets wealth" in Yoruba.

Adebowale.desc: Means "the crown has returned home" in Yoruba.

Adedayo.desc: Means "the crown becomes joy" in Yoruba.

Adegoke.desc: Means "the crown has ascended the mountain" in Yoruba.

Adekunle.desc: Means "the crown has filled the home" in Yoruba.

Adel.desc: Persian form of Adil, as well as an alternate transcription of the Arabic name.

Adela.desc: Originally a short form of names beginning with the Old German element adal meaning "noble" (Proto-Germanic *aþalaz). Saint Adela was a 7th-century Frankish princess who founded a monastery at Pfazel in France. This name was also borne by a daughter of William the Conqueror.

Adelaide.desc: Means "nobleness, nobility", from the French form of the Germanic name Adalheidis, which was composed of adal "noble" and the suffix heit "kind, sort, type". It was borne in the 10th century by Saint Adelaide, the wife of the Holy Roman emperor Otto the Great.... [more]

Adelardo.desc: Spanish and Italian form of Adalhard.

Adelbert.desc: German and Dutch variant of Adalbert.

Adele.desc: Form of Adela used in several languages. A famous bearer was the dancer and actress Adele Astaire (1896-1981). It was also borne by the British singer Adele Adkins (1988-), known simply as Adele. Shortly after she released her debut album in 2008 the name reentered the American top 1000 chart after 40-year absence.

Adelheid.desc: German and Dutch form of Adelaide.

Adélie.desc: Elaborated form of Adèle. Adélie Land in Antarctica was named in 1840 by the French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville in honour of his wife Adèle (who was sometimes called Adélie).

Adelina.desc: From a Germanic name that was derived from the element adal meaning "noble" (Proto-Germanic *aþalaz).

Adeline.desc: French and English form of Adelina.

Adelita.desc: Spanish diminutive of Adela. It is used especially in Mexico, where it is the name of a folk song about a female soldier.

Adelma.desc: Feminine form of Adelmo. This name was used by Carlo Gozzi for a character in his play Turandot (1762).

Adelmar.desc: From the Old German elements adal "noble" and mari "famous". It is a cognate of the Old English name Æðelmær.

Adelmo.desc: Italian form of Adhelm, also used to refer to the English saint Ealdhelm.

Adelyn.desc: Variant of Adeline using the popular name suffix lyn.

Adelynn.desc: Variant of Adeline using the popular name suffix lynn.

Adem.desc: Turkish, Bosnian and Albanian form of Adam.

Ademola.desc: Means "the crown is with wealth" in Yoruba.

Adenike.desc: Means "the crown is to be cared for" in Yoruba.

Adeodatus.desc: Latin name meaning "given by God". This was the name of a son of Saint Augustine and two popes (who are also known by the related name Deusdedit).

Adeola.desc: Means "the crown of wealth" in Yoruba. It is also a surname.

Aderyn.desc: Means "bird" in Welsh. This is a modern Welsh name.

Adetokunbo.desc: Means "the crown returns from over the sea" in Yoruba.

Adewale.desc: Means "the crown has come home" in Yoruba.

Adhara.desc: Derived from Arabic عذارى ('adhara) meaning "maidens". This is the name of the second brightest star (after Sirius) in the constellation Canis Major.

Adhelm.desc: From the Old German elements atto meaning "father" and helm meaning "helmet, protection".

Adi 2.desc: Means "first" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit आदि (adi).

Adi 3.desc: Diminutive of Adolf (German) or Adrian (Romanian) as well as other names beginning with the same sound.

Adil.desc: Means "fair, honest, just" in Arabic, from the root عَدَلَ ('adala) meaning "to act justly". This name was borne by several sultans of Bijapur.

Adile.desc: Turkish and Albanian feminine form of Adil.

Adilet.desc: Means "justice" in Kyrgyz and Kazakh, ultimately from Arabic عَدَلَ ('adala) meaning "to act justly".

Adin.desc: Meaning unknown, possibly from Turkish ad meaning "name".

Adina 1.desc: From Hebrew עֲדִינָא ('adina') meaning "delicate". This name is borne by a soldier in the Old Testament. It is also used in modern Hebrew as a feminine name, typically spelled עֲדִינָה.

Adina 2.desc: Meaning uncertain, possibly a short form of Adelina.

Adino.desc: Means "ornament" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament this is the name of one of King David's mighty men.

Adir.desc: Means "strong, mighty" in Hebrew. This word is used in the Hebrew Bible to describe God.

Adisa.desc: Means "bundled up and set to dry" in Yoruba.

Aditi.desc: Means "boundless, entire" or "freedom, security" in Sanskrit. This is the name of an ancient Hindu goddess of the sky and fertility. According to the Vedas she is the mother of the gods.

Aditya.desc: Means "belonging to Aditi" in Sanskrit. This is a name for the seven (or eight) Hindu gods who are the children of Aditi. It is also another name for the sun god Surya.

Adlai.desc: Contracted form of Adalia. This is the name of the father of one of King David's herdsmen in the Old Testament.

Admetus.desc: Latinized form of Greek Ἄδμητος (Admetos) meaning "unconquered, untamed", a poetic form of ἀδάμαστος (adamastos). In Greek mythology this was the name of a king of Pherae in Thessaly. He was the husband of Alcestis, who died for him.

Admir.desc: Meaning uncertain. It might be a variant of Amir 1 or it could be derived from Latin admiror meaning "admire".

Adnan.desc: Means "settler" in Arabic. According to tradition, Adnan was an ancestor of the Prophet Muhammad and the northern Arabian tribes.

Adolf.desc: From the Old German name Adalwolf, which meant "noble wolf" from the elements adal "noble" and wolf. It was borne by several Swedish kings as a first or second name, most notably by Gustav II Adolf in the 17th century. Association with Adolf Hitler (1889-1945), the leader of the Nazi party in Germany during World War II, has lessened the use of this name.

Adolfo.desc: Italian and Spanish form of Adolf.

Adolph.desc: English form of Adolf, rarely used since World War II.

Adolphe.desc: French form of Adolf, rarely used since World War II.

Adonai.desc: Means "my lord" in Hebrew. This was the title used to refer to the God of the Israelites, Yahweh, whose name was forbidden to be spoken.

Adonijah.desc: Means "my lord is Yahweh" in Hebrew. This is the name of one of King David's sons in the Old Testament. Though he was the eldest surviving son of David, he was passed over as heir to the throne in favour of Solomon.

Adoniram.desc: Means "my lord is exalted" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament this is the name of an overseer of tribute under the kings David, Solomon and Rehoboam. He was stoned to death when the Israelites revolted.

Adonis.desc: From Phoenician 𐤀𐤃𐤍 (ʾadon) meaning "lord, master". In Greek myth Adonis was a handsome young shepherd killed while hunting a wild boar. The anemone flower is said to have sprung from his blood. Because he was loved by Aphrodite, Zeus allowed him to be restored to life for part of each year. The Greeks borrowed this character from Semitic traditions, originally Sumerian (see Dumuzi).

Adoración.desc: Means "adoration" in Spanish. This name refers to the event that is known in Christian tradition as the Adoration of the Magi, which is when the three Magi presented gifts to the infant Jesus and worshipped him.

Adrastea.desc: Latinized form of Adrasteia. One of Jupiter's moons bears this name.

Adrasteia.desc: Feminine form of Adrastos. In Greek mythology this name was borne by a nymph who fostered the infant Zeus. This was also another name of the goddess Nemesis.

Adrastos.desc: Means "not inclined to run away" in Greek, from the negative prefix ἀ (a) and διδράσκω (didrasko) meaning "to run away". This was the name of a king of Argos in Greek legend.

Adrián.desc: Spanish, Hungarian and Slovak form of Hadrianus (see Hadrian).

Adrian.desc: Form of Hadrianus (see Hadrian) used in several languages. Several saints and six popes have borne this name, including the only English pope, Adrian IV, and the only Dutch pope, Adrian VI. As an English name, it has been in use since the Middle Ages, though it was not popular until modern times.

Adriana.desc: Feminine form of Adrian. A famous bearer is the Brazilian model Adriana Lima (1981-).

Adriano.desc: Italian and Portuguese form of Adrian.

Adrianus.desc: Official Dutch form of Adrian, used on birth certificates but not commonly in daily life.

Adriel.desc: Means "flock of God" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament this is the name of a man who married Saul's daughter Merab.

Adrijan.desc: Croatian and Macedonian form of Adrian.

Adrijana.desc: Slovene, Serbian, Croatian and Macedonian feminine form of Adrian.

Adsila.desc: From Cherokee ᎠᏥᎳ (atsila) "fire" or ᎠᏥᎸᏍᎩ (atsilunsgi) "flower, blossom".

Ægir.desc: Means "sea, ocean" in Old Norse. According to Norse mythology Ægir was a god or giant (jǫtunn) who lived under the ocean. His wife was Rán.

Aegle.desc: Latinized form of the Greek Αἴγλη (Aigle), which meant "light, radiance, glory". This was the name of several characters in Greek myth, including one of the Heliades and one of the Hesperides.

Ælfflæd.desc: Old English name composed of the elements ælf "elf" and flæd, possibly meaning "beauty".

Ælfgifu.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and giefu "gift". This was the name of the first wife of the English king Æðelræd II.

Ælfheah.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and heah "high". This was the name of an 11th-century archbishop of Canterbury, a saint and martyr, who is commonly known as Alphege or Elphege.

Ælfnoð.desc: Derived from the Old English element ælf "elf" combined with noð "boldness, daring".

Ælfric.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and ric "ruler, king" (making it a cognate of Alberich). This was the name of a 10th-century archbishop of Canterbury, sometimes considered a saint.

Ælfsige.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and sige "victory".

Ælfstan.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and stan "stone".

Ælfswiþ.desc: Derived from the Old English element ælf "elf" combined with swiþ "strong".

Ælfweard.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and weard "guardian".

Ælfwig.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and wig "war, battle".

Ælfwine.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and wine "friend". This name was not commonly used after the Norman Conquest.

Ælfwynn.desc: Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and wynn "joy". This name was borne by a daughter of Æðelflæd who ruled Mercia briefly in the 10th century.

Aelianus.desc: Roman cognomen that was a derivative of Aelius.

Aelita.desc: Created by Russian author Aleksey Tolstoy for his science fiction novel Aelita (1923), where it belongs to a Martian princess. In the book, the name is said to mean "starlight seen for the last time" in the Martian language.

Aelius.desc: Roman family name that was possibly derived from the Greek word ἥλιος (helios) meaning "sun". This was the family name of the Roman emperor Hadrian.

Aella.desc: Means "whirlwind" in Greek. In Greek myth this was the name of an Amazon warrior killed by Herakles during his quest for Hippolyta's girdle.

Ælred.desc: Contracted form of Æðelræd. This was the name of a 12th-century English saint.

Aeneas.desc: Latin form of the Greek name Αἰνείας (Aineias), derived from Greek αἴνη (aine) meaning "praise". In Greek legend he was a son of Aphrodite and was one of the chief heroes who defended Troy from the Greeks. The Roman poet Virgil continued his story in the Aeneid, in which Aeneas travels to Italy and founds the Roman state.

Aenoheso.desc: Means "little hawk", from Cheyenne aénohe "hawk" and the diminutive suffix -so.

Aenor.desc: Probably a Latinized form of a Germanic name of unknown meaning. This was the name of the mother of Eleanor of Aquitaine.

Aeron.desc: From the name of the Welsh river Aeron, itself probably derived from the hypothetical Celtic goddess Agrona. Alternatively, the name could be taken from Welsh aeron meaning "berries".

Aeronwen.desc: Combination of Aeron and the Welsh element gwen meaning "white, blessed".

Æsc.desc: Means "ash tree" in Old English. This was the nickname of a 5th-century king of Kent, whose birth name was Oeric.

Aeschylus.desc: From the Greek name Αἰσχύλος (Aischylos), derived from αἶσχος (aischos) meaning "shame". This was the name of a 5th-century BC Athenian playwright, known for his tragedies.

Aeson.desc: From the Greek Αἰσών (Aison), which is of unknown meaning. Aeson was the father of Jason in Greek mythology.

Aesop.desc: From the Greek Αἴσωπος (Aisopos), which is of unknown meaning. This was the name of a Greek fabulist of the 6th century BC, famous for such tales as The Tortoise and the Hare. Though his existence is uncertain, he was later said to have been a slave on the island of Samos.

Æþelbeorht.desc: Old English cognate of Adalbert (see Albert). This was the name of a Saxon king of England and two kings of Kent, one of whom was a saint. It became unused after the Normans introduced their form of Adalbert after their invasion.

Æðelflæd.desc: Old English name composed of the elements æðele "noble" and flæd, possibly meaning "beauty". This was the name of a 10th-century ruler of Mercia (a daughter of Alfred the Great).

Æðelfrið.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and friþ "peace". The name was rarely used after the Norman Conquest.

Æðelmær.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and mære "famous". A famous bearer was the 11th-century English monk Æðelmær of Malmesbury who attempted to fly with a gliding apparatus (breaking his legs in the process).

Æthelnoð.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and noð "boldness, daring".

Æðelræd.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and ræd "counsel, advice". This was the name of two Saxon kings of England including Æðelræd II "the Unready" whose realm was overrun by the Danes in the early 11th century. The name was rarely used after the Norman Conquest.

Æðelric.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and ric "ruler, king". This was the name of several early Anglo-Saxon kings.

Æðelstan.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and stan "stone". This was the name of a 10th-century English king, the first to rule all of England. The name was rarely used after the Norman Conquest, though it enjoyed a modest revival (as Athelstan) in the 19th century.

Æðelþryð.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and þryþ "strength".

Æthelweald.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and weald "powerful, mighty".

Æthelweard.desc: Derived from the Old English element æðele "noble" combined with weard "guardian".

Æðelwine.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and wine "friend". This was the name of a few Anglo-Saxon saints, including a 7th-century bishop of Lindsey. The name became rare after the Norman Conquest.

Æðelwulf.desc: Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and wulf "wolf" (making it a cognate of Adolf). This name was borne by a 9th-century king of Wessex.

Aether.desc: Latinized form of Greek Αἰθήρ (Aither) meaning "ether, heaven", derived from αἴθω (aitho) meaning "to burn, to ignite". In Greek mythology this was the name of the god of the upper sky.

Aetius.desc: Roman cognomen that was probably derived from Greek ἀετός (aetos) meaning "eagle". A famous bearer was the 5th-century Roman general Flavius Aetius, who defeated Attila the Hun at the Battle of Chalons.

Afanasy.desc: Alternate transcription of Russian Афанасий (see Afanasiy).

Afërdita.desc: Means "daybreak, morning" in Albanian, from afër "nearby, close" and ditë "day". It is also used as an Albanian form of Aphrodite.

Affan.desc: From Arabic عفّ ('aff) meaning "chaste, modest, pure". This was the name of the father of the caliph Uthman.

Afina.desc: Russian and Ukrainian form of Athena.

Afon.desc: Means "river" in Welsh. This is a Welsh name of recent origin.

Afonso.desc: Portuguese and Galician form of Alfonso. This was the name of the first king of Portugual, ruling in the 12th century.

Afra 1.desc: Originally used by the Romans as a nickname for a woman from Africa. This was the name of two early saints.

África.desc: Spanish form of Africa 1. It is usually taken from the title of the Virgin Mary, Nuestra Señora de África, the patron saint of the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in North Africa.

Africa 1.desc: From the name of the continent, which is of Latin origin, possibly from the Afri people who lived near Carthage in North Africa. This rare name is used most often by African-American parents.

Africanus.desc: Roman cognomen derived from the place name Africa, which in Roman times referred only to North Africa. This was the agnomen of the 3rd-century BC Roman general Scipio Africanus, who was honoured with it after his victory over Carthage in the Second Punic War. His descendants used it as a cognomen.

Afrodita.desc: Spanish and Russian form of Aphrodite.

Afrodite.desc: Italian and Portuguese form of Aphrodite.

Afsoon.desc: Alternate transcription of Persian افسون (see Afsoun).

Afsun.desc: Alternate transcription of Persian افسون (see Afsoun).

Agamemnon.desc: Possibly means "very steadfast" in Greek. In Greek mythology he was the brother of Menelaus. He led the Greek expedition to Troy to recover his brother's wife Helen. After the Trojan War Agamemnon was killed by his wife Clytemnestra.

Agape.desc: Derived from Greek ἀγάπη (agape) meaning "love". This name was borne by at least two early saints.

Agapetus.desc: Latinized form of the Greek name Agapetos (see Agapito).

Agapios.desc: Masculine form of Agape. This was the name of a saint from Caesarea who was martyred during the persecutions of the Roman emperor Diocletian in the early 4th century.

Agapito.desc: From the Late Latin name Agapitus or Agapetus, which was derived from the Greek name Ἀγαπητός (Agapetos) meaning "beloved". The name Agapetus was borne by two popes.

Agar.desc: Form of Hagar used in the Greek and Latin Old Testament.

Ágata.desc: Spanish and Portuguese form of Agatha.

Agáta.desc: Czech and Slovak form of Agatha.

Agata.desc: Form of Agatha in various languages.

Agatha.desc: Latinized form of the Greek name Ἀγαθή (Agathe), derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good". Saint Agatha was a 3rd-century martyr from Sicily who was tortured and killed after spurning the advances of a Roman official. The saint was widely revered in the Middle Ages, and her name has been used throughout Christian Europe (in various spellings). The mystery writer Agatha Christie (1890-1976) was a famous modern bearer of this name.

Agathangelos.desc: Means "bearer of good news", derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and ἄγγελος (angelos) meaning "messenger, angel". Saint Agathangelus of Rome was a 4th-century deacon who was martyred during the persecutions of the emperor Diocletian.

Agathe.desc: Form of Agatha in several languages.

Agathinus.desc: Latinized form of Greek Ἀγαθίνος (Agathinos), derived from ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good".

Agaue.desc: Means "illustrious, noble" in Greek. This was the mother of Pentheus in Greek myth.

Agilulf.desc: Old German name derived from the elements agil meaning "edge, blade" and wolf meaning "wolf". This name was borne by a 6th-century king of the Lombards and by an 8th-century saint (a bishop of Cologne).

Agimar.desc: Derived from the Old Frankish element aggju, Old High German ekka meaning "edge, blade" combined with mari meaning "famous".

Aglaia.desc: Means "splendour, beauty" in Greek. In Greek mythology she was one of the three Graces or Χάριτες (Charites). This name was also borne by a 4th-century saint from Rome.

Agnar.desc: From the Old Norse name Agnarr, derived from agi "awe, fear" or egg "edge of a sword" combined with herr "army, warrior".

Agnès.desc: French and Catalan form of Agnes.

Agnes.desc: Latinized form of the Greek name Ἁγνή (Hagne), derived from Greek ἁγνός (hagnos) meaning "chaste". Saint Agnes was a virgin martyred during the persecutions of the Roman emperor Diocletian. The name became associated with Latin agnus "lamb", resulting in the saint's frequent depiction with a lamb by her side. Due to her renown, the name became common in Christian Europe.... [more]

Agnesa.desc: Slovak and Albanian form of Agnes.

Agnese.desc: Italian and Latvian form of Agnes.

Agnete.desc: Danish and Norwegian variant of Agnes.

Agnethe.desc: Danish and Norwegian variant of Agnes.

Agni 1.desc: Means "fire" in Sanskrit. This is the name of the ancient Hindu fire god, usually depicted as red-skinned with three legs, seven arms, and two faces.

Agnia.desc: Alternate transcription of Russian Агния (see Agniya).

Agnija.desc: Serbian, Macedonian and Latvian form of Agnes.

Ago.desc: From the Old High German element ekka, Old Saxon eggia meaning "edge, blade" (Proto-Germanic *agjō). Alternatively it could be from Old High German egi meaning "fear" (Proto-Germanic *agaz). This was the name of a 7th-century Duke of Friuli.

Agostina.desc: Italian feminine form of Augustinus (see Augustine 1).

Agrippa.desc: Roman cognomen of unknown meaning, possibly from a combination of Greek ἄγριος (agrios) meaning "wild" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse" or alternatively of Etruscan origin. It was also used as a praenomen, or given name, by the Furia and Menenia families. In the New Testament this name was borne by Herod Agrippa (a grandson of Herod the Great), the king of Israel who put the apostle James to death. It was also borne by the 1st-century BC Roman general Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa.

Agrippina.desc: Feminine derivative of Agrippa. This name was borne by the scheming mother of the Roman emperor Nero, who eventually had her killed. This was also the name of a 3rd-century Roman saint who is venerated in Sicily.

Agron.desc: Probably of Illyrian origin, maybe related to Albanian ag meaning "dawn". Alternatively it might be connected to Greek ἀγρός (agros) meaning "field". This was the name of a 3rd-century BC Illyrian king, the husband of Teuta.

Agrona.desc: Perhaps derived from the old Celtic root *agro- meaning "battle, slaughter". This is possibly the name of a Brythonic goddess for whom the River Ayr in Scotland and River Aeron in Wales were named.

Águeda.desc: Spanish and Portuguese form of Agatha.

Agustina.desc: Spanish feminine form of Augustinus (see Augustine 1).

Ah.desc: From the Chinese character 阿 (ā), which has no distinct meaning. It is not normally given as a name, but it can be prefixed to another name to make it a diminutive.

Ahab.desc: Means "uncle", from Hebrew אָח ('ach) meaning "brother" and אָב ('av) meaning "father". This was the name of a king of Israel, the husband of Jezebel, as told in the Old Testament. He was admonished by Elijah for his sinful behaviour. Herman Melville later used this name in his novel Moby-Dick (1851), where it belongs to a sea captain obsessively hunting for a white whale.

Ahasuerus.desc: From Hebrew אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ ('Achashwerosh), from the Old Persian name Xšayarša (see Xerxes). This name appears several times in the Old Testament belonging to a king of Persia. In the Book of Esther, Ahasuerus is the husband of Esther.

Ahenobarbus.desc: From a Roman cognomen meaning "bronze beard" in Latin. This name was borne by a series of consuls of the late Roman Republic.

Ahinoam.desc: Means "my brother is pleasant" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament this is the name of wives of both Saul and David.

Ahmad.desc: Means "most commendable, most praiseworthy" in Arabic (a superlative form of Hamid 1).

Ahmed.desc: Variant of Ahmad. This was the name of three Ottoman sultans.

Ahmose.desc: From Egyptian jꜥḥ-ms meaning "born of Iah", derived from the name of the Egyptian god Iah combined with msj meaning "be born". This was the name of the first pharaoh of the 18th dynasty (16th century BC). He defeated the Hyksos and drove them from Egypt. It was also borne by others among Egyptian royalty from the same era, including several queens consort.

Aholibamah.desc: Means "tent of the high place" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament this is one of the wives of Esau, possibly the same as Judith.

Ahoth.desc: Form of Ehud used in the Latin Old Testament.

Ahriman.desc: Modern Persian form of Angra Mainyu.

Ahtahkakoop.desc: From Cree ᐊᑖᐦᑲᑯᐦᑊ (Atâhkakohp) meaning "star blanket", derived from ᐊᑖᕁ (atâhk) "star" and ᐊᑯᐦᑊ (akohp) "blanket". This was the name of an early 19th-century chief of a Plains Cree people.

Ahti.desc: Meaning unknown. This is the name of the Finnish god of the ocean, rivers and fishing.

Ahuludegi.desc: Means "he throws away the drum" from Cherokee ᎠᎱᎵ (ahuli) "drum" and ᎤᏕᎦ (udega) "throw". This was the name of a 19th-century Cherokee chief, also known as John Jolly.

Ahura Mazda.desc: Means "lord of wisdom", from Avestan 𐬀𐬵𐬎𐬭𐬀 (ahura) meaning "lord" and 𐬨𐬀𐬰𐬛𐬁 (mazdā) meaning "wisdom". In Zoroastrianism Ahura Mazda was the supreme creator, and the god of light, truth, and goodness.

Ai 1.desc: From Japanese 愛 (ai) meaning "love, affection", 藍 (ai) meaning "indigo", or other kanji with the same pronunciation.

Ai 2.desc: From Chinese 爱 (ài) meaning "love, affection", 蔼 (ǎi) meaning "friendly, lush", or other characters that are pronounced similarly.

Aibek.desc: Derived from Kazakh and Kyrgyz ай (ay) meaning "moon" combined with the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".

Aïcha.desc: Form of Aisha used in Northern Africa and other French-influenced regions of the continent.

Aïchatou.desc: Form of Aisha used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.

Aida.desc: Variant of Ayda. This name was used in Verdi's opera Aida (1871), where it belongs to an Ethiopian princess held captive in Egypt.

Aidan.desc: Anglicized form of Aodhán. In the latter part of the 20th century it became popular in America due to its sound, since it shares a sound with such names as Braden and Hayden. It peaked ranked 39th for boys in 2003.

Aidana.desc: Means "wise moon" in Kazakh, from ай (ay) meaning "moon" and дана (dana) meaning "wise".

Aiday.desc: Means "moon-like" in Kazakh, from ай (ay) meaning "moon" and the suffix дай (day) meaning "like".

Aifric.desc: From Old Irish Affraic, possibly from Afraicc, the Old Irish name of the continent of Africa (see Africa 1). Alternatively, it could be from *Aithbrecc, an unattested earlier form of Aithbhreac. This was the name of two abbesses of Kildare in the 8th and 9th centuries. It was also borne by a 12th-century daughter of the king of the Isle of Mann who married the Anglo-Norman knight John de Courcy.

Aigar.desc: Possibly from the Finnic root aika meaning "time" (Estonian aeg).

Aigars.desc: Probably from a Livonian name that was a cognate of Aigar.

Aigerim.desc: Means "wonderful moon", from Kazakh ай (ay) meaning "moon" and керім (kerim) meaning "wonderful".

Aigul.desc: Kazakh and Kyrgyz form of Aygül.

Aija.desc: Of uncertain meaning, possibly related to Latvian aijāt meaning "to rock, to lull". It was used by the Latvian writer Jānis Jaunsudrabiņš for the title character of his novel Aija (1911).

Aikaterini.desc: Alternate transcription of Greek Αικατερίνη (see Ekaterini).

Aike.desc: Diminutive of names beginning with the Old German element ekka meaning "edge, blade" or adal meaning "noble".

Aiko.desc: From Japanese 愛 (ai) meaning "love, affection" and 子 (ko) meaning "child", as well as other character combinations.

Aikorkem.desc: Means "elegant moon", derived from Kazakh ай (ay) meaning "moon" and көркем (korkem) meaning "elegant, graceful, refined, artistic".

Ailbhe.desc: From Old Irish Ailbe, possibly derived from the old Celtic root *albiyo- "world, light, white" or Old Irish ail "rock". In Irish legend this was the name of a female warrior of the Fianna. It was also the name of a 6th-century masculine saint, the founder of a monastery at Emly.

Aili.desc: Finnish and Estonian form of Áile.

Ailill.desc: Means "elf" in Irish. This name was borne by several early Irish kings. It also occurs frequently in Irish legend, borne for example by the husband of Queen Medb.

Ailín.desc: Possibly an Irish form of Alan or Ælfwine.

Ailsa.desc: From Ailsa Craig, the name of an island off the west coast of Scotland, which is of uncertain derivation.

Aiman 1.desc: Means "beauty of the moon" in Kazakh.

Aiman 2.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic أيمن (see Ayman).

Aimar.desc: Medieval Basque name, possibly derived from the Germanic name Agimar.

Aimé.desc: From Old French Amé, the masculine form of Amée (see Amy).

Aimee.desc: Variant of Amy, influenced by French Aimée.

Aimeric.desc: Probably a variant of Heimirich. Aimeric (or Aimery) was the name of several viscounts of Narbonne between the 11th and 13th centuries. It was also borne by the first king of Cyprus (12th century), originally from Poitou, France.

Aimi.desc: From Japanese 愛 (ai) meaning "love, affection" and 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful". Other combinations of kanji characters are possible.

Aimilios.desc: Alternate transcription of Greek Αιμίλιος (see Emilios).

Ain.desc: Possibly an Estonian short form of Hendrik.

Aina 1.desc: Variant of Aino. It also means "always" in Finnish.

Aina 3.desc: From Japanese 愛 (ai) meaning "love, affection" and 菜 (na) meaning "vegetables, greens", as well as other character combinations.

Aina 5.desc: Means "mirror" in Kazakh, ultimately from Persian آینه (ayneh).

Áine.desc: Means "radiance, brilliance" in Irish. This was the name of a goddess of love and fertility in Irish legend, thought to dwell at the hill of Cnoc Áine in Limerick. It has sometimes been Anglicized as Anne.

Ainhoa.desc: From the name of a town in southwest France where there is a famous image of the Virgin Mary.

Aino.desc: Means "the only one" in Finnish. In the Finnish epic the Kalevala this is the name of a girl who drowns herself when she finds out she must marry the old man Väinämöinen.

Ainsley.desc: From an English surname that was from a place name: either Annesley in Nottinghamshire or Ansley in Warwickshire. The place names themselves derive from Old English anne "alone, solitary" or ansetl "hermitage" and leah "woodland, clearing".... [more]

Aiolos.desc: Means "quick-moving, nimble" in Greek. This was the name of the Greek god of the winds.

Airat.desc: Alternate transcription of Tatar/Bashkir Айрат (see Ayrat).

Airi 1.desc: From Japanese 愛 (ai) meaning "love, affection" combined with 莉 (ri) meaning "white jasmine" or 梨 (ri) meaning "pear". Other combinations of kanji characters are possible.

Airi 2.desc: From Finnish airut meaning "messenger, herald", also influenced by place names beginning with the same sound.

'Aisha.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عائشة (see Aisha).

A'isha.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عائشة (see Aisha).

Aisha.desc: Means "living, alive" in Arabic. This was the name of Muhammad's third wife, the daughter of Abu Bakr. Some time after Muhammad's death she went to war against Ali, the fourth caliph, but was defeated. Her name is used more by Sunni Muslims and less by Shias.... [more]

Aishah.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عائشة (see Aisha), as well as the usual Malay form.

Aishwarya.desc: Means "prosperity, wealth" in Sanskrit. A famous bearer is the Indian actress Aishwarya Rai Bachchan (1973-).

Aisling.desc: Means "dream" or "vision" in Irish. This name was created in the 20th century.

Aïssa.desc: Form of Aisha used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.

Aïssatou.desc: Form of Aisha used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.

Aistė.desc: From the name of the Baltic tribe of the Aesti, mentioned by the Roman historian Tacitus, called the Aisçiai in Lithuanian.

Aisultan.desc: Derived from Kazakh ай (ay) meaning "moon" and сұлтан (sultan) meaning "sultan, king" (of Arabic origin).

Aitana.desc: From the name of a mountain range in Valencia, eastern Spain. The Spanish poet Rafael Alberti used it for his daughter in 1941.

Aithan.desc: Form of Ethan used in the Greek Old Testament.

Aithbhreac.desc: Older form of Oighrig. This name was borne by the 15th-century Scottish poet Aithbhreac Inghean Coirceadal.

Aitor.desc: Possibly means "good fathers" from Basque aita "father" and on "good". This was the name of a legendary ancestor of the Basques.

Aivars.desc: Latvian form of Ivar. The Latvian author Vilis Lācis used it for a character in his novel Uz Jauno Krastu (1952).

Aiza.desc: Meaning unknown, possibly of Arabic origin.

Aizah.desc: Alternate transcription of Urdu عائزہ (see Aiza).

Aizere.desc: Means "golden moon" from Kazakh ай (ay) meaning "moon" and Persian زر (zar) meaning "gold".

Ajax.desc: From the Greek name Αἴας (Aias), perhaps deriving from Greek αἰαστής (aiastes) meaning "mourner" or αἶα (aia) meaning "earth, land". In Greek mythology this was the name of two of the heroes who fought for the Greeks in the Trojan War, the son of Telamon and the son of Oileus. When the armour of the slain hero Achilles was not given to Ajax Telamonian, he became mad with jealousy and killed himself.

Ajay.desc: Means "unconquered", from Sanskrit अ (a) meaning "not" and जय (jaya) meaning "victory, conquest".

Ajeet.desc: Alternate transcription of Hindi अजीत, Marathi अजित, Gurmukhi ਅਜੀਤ or Bengali অজিত (see Ajit).

Ajit.desc: Means "unconquered, invincible", from Sanskrit अ (a) meaning "not" and जित (jita) meaning "conquered". This is a name of the gods Shiva and Vishnu, and of a future Buddha.

Ajla.desc: Bosnian and Albanian form of Ayla 2.

Akachi.desc: Means "the hand of God" in Igbo.

Akakios.desc: From a Greek word meaning "innocent, not evil", derived from ἀ (a), a negative prefix, combined with κάκη (kake) meaning "evil". This was the name of three early saints, two of whom were martyred.

Akane.desc: From Japanese 茜 (akane) meaning "deep red, dye from the rubia plant". Other kanji or combinations of kanji can form this name as well.

Akari.desc: From Japanese 明 (aka) meaning "bright" or 朱 (aka) meaning "vermilion red" combined with 里 (ri) meaning "village" or 莉 (ri) meaning "white jasmine". Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.

Akbar.desc: Means "greater, greatest" in Arabic. This was the name of a 16th-century Mughal ruler who expanded the empire to include most of India.

Akemi.desc: From Japanese 明 (ake) meaning "bright" and 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Akhenaton.desc: From Egyptian ꜣḫ-n-jtn meaning "effective for Aton". Akhenaton was a 14th-century BC Egyptian pharaoh of the New Kingdom, who is best known for promoting the monotheistic worship of the sun god Aton. He changed his name from Amenhotep in order to honour the god. After his death, polytheism resumed.

Akhmad.desc: Chechen, Ingush and Indonesian form of Ahmad.

Akhmat.desc: Bashkir and Tatar form of Ahmad.

Áki.desc: Old Norse diminutive of names containing the element anu "ancestor".

Aki 2.desc: From Japanese 晶 (aki) meaning "clear, crystal", 明 (aki) meaning "bright, light, clear" or 秋 (aki) meaning "autumn". It can also come from 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia" combined with 希 (ki) meaning "hope". Other kanji or combinations of kanji can form this name too.

Akiba.desc: Alternate transcription of Hebrew עֲקִיבָא (see Akiva).

Akicita.desc: From Lakota or Dakota akíčhita meaning "warrior".

Akie.desc: From Japanese 秋 (aki) meaning "autumn" or 昭 (aki) meaning "bright" combined with 絵 (e) meaning "picture, painting" or 恵 (e) meaning "favour, benefit". Other kanji combinations can also form this name.

Akihiko.desc: From Japanese 明 (aki) or 昭 (aki) both meaning "bright" combined with 彦 (hiko) meaning "boy, prince". Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.

Akihito.desc: From Japanese 明 (aki) or 昭 (aki) both meaning "bright" combined with 仁 (hito) meaning "compassionate". Other kanji combinations are possible. Akihito (1933-), name written 明仁, was the emperor of Japan from 1989 to 2019.

Akiko.desc: From Japanese 晶 (aki) meaning "clear, crystal", 明 (aki) meaning "bright, light, clear" or 秋 (aki) meaning "autumn" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other combinations of kanji characters are possible.

Akilah.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic عقيلة or عاقلة (see Aqila).

Akilina.desc: Russian form of the Roman name Aquilina, a feminine derivative of Aquila.

Akimitsu.desc: From Japanese 昭 (aki) meaning "bright" and 光 (mitsu) meaning "light". Other combinations of kanji can also form this name.

Akinyi.desc: Means "born in the morning" in Luo.

Akio.desc: From Japanese 昭 (aki) meaning "bright, luminous" combined with 夫 (o) meaning "man, husband", 男 (o) meaning "male, man" or 雄 (o) meaning "hero, manly". Other kanji combinations are also possible.

Akira.desc: From Japanese 昭 (akira) meaning "bright", 明 (akira) meaning "bright" or 亮 (akira) meaning "clear". Other kanji with the same pronunciation can also form this name. A famous bearer was the Japanese filmmaker Akira Kurosawa (1910-1998), given name written 明.

Akito.desc: From Japanese 章 (aki) meaning "chapter" combined with 斗 (to), which refers to a Chinese constellation, or 人 (to) meaning "person". Other kanji combinations can also form this name.

Akiva.desc: From an Aramaic form of Yaakov. Akiva (or Akiba) ben Joseph was a prominent 1st-century Jewish rabbi.

Akmad.desc: Maguindanao and Tausug form of Ahmad.

Akmal.desc: Means "more perfect, more complete" in Arabic, a comparative form of كامل (kamil).

Akmaral.desc: Derived from Kazakh ақ (aq) meaning "white" and марал (maral) meaning "deer".

Ákos.desc: Possibly of Turkic origin meaning "white falcon". This was the name of a medieval Hungarian clan.

Akram.desc: Means "most generous" in Arabic (a superlative form of Karim).

Aksinia.desc: Bulgarian form of Xenia, as well as an alternate transcription of Russian Аксинья (see Aksinya).

Al.desc: Short form of Albert and other names beginning with Al. A notable bearer is American actor Al Pacino (1940-).

Ala 2.desc: Means "earth, land" in Igbo. In traditional Igbo religion Ala (called Ani or Ana in other dialects) is an earth goddess associated with fertility and ancestors.

Ala ad-Din.desc: Means "excellence of religion" from Arabic عَلَاء ('ala) meaning "excellence, elevation" combined with دين (din) meaning "religion, faith". This was the name of several sultans of Delhi.

Ala al-Din.desc: Alternate transcription of Arabic علاء الدين (see Ala ad-Din).

Alaba.desc: Means "second child after twins" in Yoruba.

Aladdin.desc: Anglicized form of Ala ad-Din. This is the name of a mischievous boy in one of the tales of The 1001 Nights. A magician traps him in a cave, but he escapes with the help of a genie.

Alaia 2.desc: Probably a variant of Alayah. It is likely also influenced by the fashion brand Alaïa, named for the Tunisian-French designer Azzedine Alaïa (1935-2017). His surname in Arabic is عليّة ('Alayyah), meaning "lofty".

Alaina.desc: Variant of Alana, probably influenced by Elaine.

Al-Amir.desc: Means "the commander, the prince" in Arabic. This was the name of a 10th-century Fatimid imam.

Alan.desc: The meaning of this name is not known for certain. It was used in Brittany at least as early as the 6th century, and it possibly means either "little rock" or "handsome" in Breton. Alternatively, it may derive from the tribal name of the Alans, an Iranian people who migrated into Europe in the 4th and 5th centuries.... [more]

Alani.desc: Possibly a variant of Alana, or possibly from Hawaiian ʻalani meaning "orange (tree or fruit)".

Alanis.desc: Feminine form of Alan. Canadian musician Alanis Morissette (1974-) was named after her father Alan. Her parents apparently decided to use this particular spelling after seeing this word in a Greek newspaper.

Alannah.desc: Variant of Alana. It has been influenced by the affectionate Anglo-Irish word alannah, from the Irish Gaelic phrase a leanbh meaning "O child".

Alaric.desc: From the Gothic name *Alareiks meaning "ruler of all", derived from the element alls "all" combined with reiks "ruler, king". This was the name of a king of the Visigoths who sacked Rome in the 5th century.

Alassane.desc: Form of Al-Hasan used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.

Alastor.desc: Means "avenger" in Greek. This was an epithet of Zeus, as well as the name of several other characters from Greek mythology.

Alaya.desc: Variant of Alayah. It coincides with a Buddhist term (meaning "dwelling" in Sanskrit), which refers to the eighth level of human consciousness.

Alayah.desc: Probably a variant of Aaliyah based on names such as Amaya and Anaya.

Alazne.desc: From Basque alatz meaning "miracle". It is an equivalent of Milagros, proposed by Sabino Arana in his 1910 list of Basque saints names.

Alba 1.desc: This name is derived from two distinct names, Alba 2 and Alba 3, with distinct origins, Latin and Germanic. Over time these names have become confused with one another. To further complicate the matter, alba means "dawn" in Italian, Spanish and Catalan. This may be the main inspiration behind its use in Italy and Spain.

Alba 3.desc: Originally a short form of Germanic names beginning with the element alb meaning "elf" (Proto-Germanic *albaz).

Albaer.desc: Limburgish form of Albert. Its spelling has been influenced by the French pronunciation of Albert.

Alban.desc: From the Roman cognomen Albanus, which meant "from Alba". Alba (from Latin albus "white") was the name of various places within the Roman Empire, including the city Alba Longa. This name was borne by Saint Alban, the first British martyr (4th century). According to tradition, he sheltered a fugitive priest in his house. When his house was searched, he disguised himself as the priest, was arrested in his stead, and was beheaded. Another 4th-century martyr by this name was Saint Alban of Mainz.... [more]

Albano.desc: Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Albanus (see Alban).

Albarīks.desc: Proto-Germanic reconstruction of Alberich, Ælfric and Alfríkr.

Albaweniz.desc: Proto-Germanic reconstruction of Ælfwine, Alboin and Alfvin.

Albena.desc: Created by Bulgarian writer Yordan Yovkov for the heroine in his drama Albena (1930). He may have based it on ablen, the name of a type of peony (a flowering plant).

Alberich.desc: Derived from the Old German elements alb "elf" and rih "ruler, king". It was borne by two Lombard dukes of Spoleto in the 10th century. It was also the name of a 12th-century French saint who helped found the Cistercian Order.... [more]

Albert.desc: From the Germanic name Adalbert meaning "noble and bright", composed of the elements adal "noble" and beraht "bright". This name was common among medieval German royalty. The Normans introduced it to England, where it replaced the Old English cognate Æþelbeorht. Though it became rare in England by the 17th century, it was repopularized in the 19th century by the German-born Prince Albert, the husband of Queen Victoria.... [more]

Alberta.desc: Feminine form of Albert. This is the name of a Canadian province, which was named in honour of a daughter of Queen Victoria.

Alberte 2.desc: French and Danish feminine form of Albert.

Alberto.desc: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Albert.

Albertus.desc: Latinized form of Albert. This is the official Dutch form of the name, used on birth certificates but commonly rendered Albert in daily life.

Albin.desc: Form of Albinus in several languages.

Albína.desc: Czech and Slovak form of Albina.

Albina.desc: Feminine form of Albinus. This was the name of a few early saints, including a 3rd-century martyr from Caesarea.

Albino.desc: Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Albinus.

Albinus.desc: Roman cognomen that was a derivative of Albus. Saint Albinus (also called Aubin) was a 6th-century bishop of Angers in Brittany.

Alboin.desc: From the Old German elements alb "elf" and wini "friend". It is a cognate of Ælfwine. This was the name of a 6th-century king of the Lombards who began the Lombard conquest of Italy.

Alborz.desc: From the name of a mountain range (of unknown etymology) in northern Iran.

Albus.desc: Roman cognomen meaning "white, bright" in Latin.

Alcaeus.desc: Latinized form of the Greek name Ἀλκαῖος (Alkaios) meaning "strong", derived from ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess". This was the name of a 7th-century BC lyric poet from the island of Lesbos.

Alcestis.desc: Latinized form of Greek Ἄλκηστις (Alkestis), derived from ἀλκηστής (alkestes) meaning "brave, valiant", a derivative of ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess". In Greek mythology she was the wife of King Admetus. She offered to die in place of her husband, though she was eventually rescued from the underworld by Herakles. This story was told by the Greek playwright Euripides in his 5th-century BC tragedy Alcestis.

Alcibiades.desc: Latinized form of the Greek name Ἀλκιβιάδης (Alkibiades), derived from ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" and βία (bia) meaning "force" with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides). This was the name of a notable Greek statesman and general during the Peloponnesian War. He changed allegiance from Athens to Sparta and back again during the course of the war. He features in Shakespeare's tragedy Timon of Athens (1607).

Alcide.desc: Italian and French form of Alcides.

Alcides.desc: Latinized form of Greek Ἀλκείδης (Alkeides), derived from ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" and the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides). This was another name for the hero Herakles.

Alcippe.desc: From Greek Ἀλκίππη (Alkippe), derived from ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse". This was the name of a daughter of Ares in Greek myth. Her father killed Halirrhotis, a son of Poseidon, when he attempted to rape her, leading to a murder trial in which Ares was quickly acquitted.

Alcmene.desc: From Greek Ἀλκμήνη (Alkmene), derived from ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" combined with μήνη (mene) meaning "moon" or μῆνις (menis) meaning "wrath". In Greek mythology Alcmene was the wife of Amphitryon. She was the mother of Herakles by Zeus, who bedded her by disguising himself as her absent husband.

Alcyone.desc: Latinized form of Greek Ἀλκυόνη (Alkyone), derived from the word ἀλκυών (alkyon) meaning "kingfisher". In Greek myth this name belonged to a daughter of Aeolus and the wife of Ceyx. After her husband was killed in a shipwreck she threw herself into the water, but the gods saved her and turned them both into kingfishers. This is also the name of the brightest of the Pleiades, a group of stars in the constellation Taurus, supposedly the daughters of Atlas and Pleione.

Aldara.desc: Galician form of the Visigothic name *Hildiwara, which was composed of the Gothic elements hilds "battle" and wars "aware, cautious". This was the name of the 7th-century wife of the Visigothic king Gundemar. It was also borne by the mother of Saint Rosendo (10th century).

Aldebrand.desc: Old German name derived from the elements alt meaning "old" and brant meaning "fire, torch, sword". Saint Aldebrand was a 12th-century bishop of Fossombrone in Italy.

Aldegar.desc: Derived from the Old German elements alt "old" and ger "spear".

Aldegund.desc: Germanic name, derived from the elements alt "old" and gunda "war". Alternatively, it could be a metathesized form of Adalgund. Saint Aldegund (or Aldegundis or Adelgundis) was a 7th-century Frankish abbess at Maubeuge.

Alden.desc: From a surname that was derived from the Old English given name Ealdwine.

Aldert.desc: Frisian form of a Germanic name, either Aldhard or Adalhard.

Aldhard.desc: Derived from the Old German elements alt "old" and hart "hard, firm, brave, hardy".

Aldina 2.desc: Bosnian feminine form of Ala ad-Din.

Aldiyar.desc: Derived from the archaic Kazakh title алдияр (aldiyar), which was used to address a ruler (equivalent to English Your Majesty). The word is ultimately of Persian origin, but of uncertain meaning.

Aldo.desc: Originally a short form of Germanic names beginning with the element alt meaning "old" (Proto-Germanic *aldaz), and sometimes also with adal meaning "noble" (Proto-Germanic *aþalaz).

Aldona.desc: Meaning unknown. This was the name of a 14th-century Polish queen, the daughter of a Grand Duke of Lithuania.

Aldous.desc: Probably a diminutive of names beginning with the Old English element eald "old". It has been in use as an English given name since the Middle Ages, mainly in East Anglia. The British author Aldous Huxley (1894-1963) was a famous bearer of this name.

Aldric.desc: From a Germanic name, derived from the elements alt "old" and rih "ruler, king". Saint Aldric was a 9th-century bishop of Le Mans.

Aldwin.desc: Derived from the Old German elements alt "old" and wini "friend". This is a cognate of Old English Ealdwine.

Ale 1.desc: Finnish short form of Aleksanteri or Aleksi, an Italian short form of Alessandro, and a Spanish short form of Alejandro or Alejandra.

Ale 2.desc: Originally a short form of Germanic names beginning with the element adal meaning "noble".

Alecto.desc: Latinized form of Greek Ἀληκτώ (Alekto), which was derived from ἄληκτος (alektos) meaning "unceasing". This was the name of one of the Furies or Ἐρινύες (Erinyes) in Greek mythology.

Aled.desc: From the name of a Welsh river, of uncertain meaning.

Aleixo.desc: Portuguese and Galician form of Alexis.

Alejandro.desc: Spanish form of Alexander. This was the most popular name for boys in Spain from the 1990s until 2006 (and again in 2011).

Aleks.desc: Short form of Aleksey, Aleksandr or Aleksandra.

Aleksandar.desc: Form of Alexander in several languages.

Aleksander.desc: Form of Alexander in several languages.

Aleksandr.desc: Russian and Armenian form of Alexander. This name was borne by the 19th-century Russian poet Aleksandr Pushkin.

Aleksandra.desc: Form of Alexandra in several languages.

Aleksei.desc: Alternate transcription of Russian Алексей (see Aleksey).

Aleksey.desc: Russian form of Alexis. This was the name of a 17th-century czar of Russia.

Aleksi.desc: Finnish, Bulgarian and Georgian form of Alexis.

Alemayehu.desc: Means "I have seen the world" in Amharic.

Alen.desc: Croatian, Slovene and Armenian form of Alan.

Alena 1.desc: Short form of Magdalena or Helena. This was the name of a saint, possibly legendary, who was martyred near Brussels in the 7th century.

Alessandro.desc: Italian form of Alexander. A famous bearer was Alessandro Volta (1745-1827), the Italian physicist who invented the battery.

Aleta.desc: Possibly a variant of Alethea. This was the name of the wife of the title character in the comic strip Prince Valiant, which first appeared in 1937.

Alethea.desc: Derived from Greek ἀλήθεια (aletheia) meaning "truth". This name was coined in the 16th century.

Alex.desc: Short form of Alexander, Alexandra and other names beginning with Alex.

Alexander.desc: Latinized form of the Greek name Ἀλέξανδρος (Alexandros), which meant "defending men" from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, help" and ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man" (genitive ἀνδρός). In Greek mythology this was another name of the hero Paris, and it also belongs to several characters in the New Testament. However, the most famous bearer was Alexander the Great, king of Macedon. In the 4th century BC he built a huge empire out of Greece, Egypt, Persia, and parts of India. Due to his fame, and later medieval tales involving him, use of his name spread throughout Europe.... [more]

Alexandr.desc: Czech form of Alexander, as well as an alternate transcription of Russian Александр (see Aleksandr).

Alexandra.desc: Feminine form of Alexander. In Greek mythology this was a Mycenaean epithet of the goddess Hera, and an alternate name of Cassandra. It was borne by several early Christian saints, and also by the wife of Nicholas II, the last czar of Russia. She was from Germany and had the birth name Alix, but was renamed Александра (Aleksandra) upon joining the Russian Church.

Alexandre.desc: Form of Alexander in several languages. This name was borne by the 19th-century French author Alexandre Dumas (1802-1870), who wrote The Three Musketeers.

Alexandria.desc: Feminine form of Alexander. Alexander the Great founded several cities by this name (or renamed them) as he extended his empire eastward. The most notable of these is Alexandria in Egypt, founded by Alexander in 331 BC.

Alexandrina.desc: Elaborated form of Alexandra. This was the first name of Queen Victoria; her middle name was Victoria.

Alexandrine.desc: French diminutive of Alexandra. This was the name of a Danish queen, the wife of King Christian X.

Alexei.desc: Alternate transcription of Russian Алексей (see Aleksey).

Alexej.desc: Czech and Slovak form of Alexis.

Alexey.desc: Alternate transcription of Russian Алексей (see Aleksey).

Alexina.desc: Feminine form of Alex, or a diminutive of Alexis.

Alexis.desc: From the Greek name Ἄλεξις (Alexis) meaning "helper" or "defender", derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help". This was the name of a 3rd-century BC Greek comic poet, and also of several saints. It is used somewhat interchangeably with the related name Ἀλέξιος or Alexius, borne by five Byzantine emperors. In the English-speaking world it is more commonly used as a feminine name.

Alexius.desc: Latinized form of the Greek name Ἀλέξιος (Alexios), a derivative of Ἄλεξις (see Alexis). This was the name of five Byzantine emperors. It was also borne by a 5th-century Syrian saint who is especially venerated in the Eastern Church.

Alexsandr.desc: Alternate transcription of Russian Александр (see Aleksandr).

Aleyna.desc: From Arabic علينا ('alayna) meaning "on us", a word from the Quran.

Alf 1.desc: Derived from Old Norse alfr meaning "elf". In Norse legend this was the name of king, the suitor of a reluctant maiden named Alfhild. She avoided marrying him by disguising herself as a warrior, but when they fought she was so impressed by his strength that she changed her mind.

Alfbern.desc: Derived from the Old German elements alb "elf" and bern "bear".

Alfhard.desc: Old German name composed of the elements alb "elf" and hart "hard, firm, brave, hardy".

Alfher.desc: Old German name composed of the elements alb "elf" and heri "army" (making it a cognate of Alvar).

Alfhild.desc: From the Old Norse name Alfhildr, which was composed of the elements alfr "elf" and hildr "battle". In Scandinavian legend Alfhild was a maiden who disguised herself as a warrior in order to avoid marriage to King Alf. Her life was perhaps based on that of a 9th-century Viking pirate.

Alfia.desc: Possibly derived from Arabic ألْف (alf) meaning "thousand". Alternatively, it may be of Turkic origin.

Alfiya.desc: Alternate transcription of Tatar Әлфия (see Alfia).

Alfons.desc: German, Dutch and Catalan form of Alfonso.

Alfonso.desc: Spanish and Italian form of Alphonsus, the Latin form of the Visigothic name *Aþalafuns meaning "noble and ready", derived from the Gothic elements aþals "noble" and funs "ready". This was the name of several kings of Spain (Asturias, León, Castile and Aragon) and Portugal, starting with Alfonso I of Asturias in the 8th century. His name was sometimes recorded in the Latin spelling Adefonsus, and on that basis it is theorized that first element might be from another source (perhaps haþus meaning "battle"). It is possible that two or more names merged into a single form.

Alfonz.desc: Slovak, Slovene and Hungarian form of Alfonso.

Alfréd.desc: Hungarian, Slovak and Czech form of Alfred.

Alfred.desc: Means "elf counsel", derived from the Old English name Ælfræd, composed of the elements ælf "elf" and ræd "counsel, advice". Alfred the Great was a 9th-century king of Wessex who fought unceasingly against the Danes living in northeast England. He was also a scholar, and he translated many Latin books into Old English. His fame helped to ensure the usage of this name even after the Norman Conquest, when most Old English names were replaced by Norman ones. It became rare by the end of the Middle Ages, but was revived in the 18th century.... [more]

Alfredo.desc: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Alfred.

Alfríkr.desc: Derived from the Old Norse elements alfr "elf" and ríkr "ruler, king" (making it a cognate of Alberich).

Alfvin.desc: From the Old Norse elements alfr "elf" and vinr "friend". It is a cognate of Ælfwine.

Algar.desc: Means "elf spear" from Old English ælf "elf" and gar "spear". This Old English name was rarely used after the Norman Conquest, being absorbed by similar-sounding names and Norman and Scandinavian cognates. It was briefly revived in the 19th century.
